lede: Weigh a crate of eggs, measure a hundred arm spans, or time the same journey again and again, and the results pile up in one shape: a hump in the middle, falling away evenly on both sides. This lesson is about that shape, the normal curve, and the shares of it that every normal curve keeps.
can: Recognise a variable that is roughly normal, and one that is not
Use the curve's symmetry: mean, median and mode together, half on each side
Use the 68%, 95% and 99.7% shares to find ranges and the share in one tail

md: Plot a lot of one measured quantity, such as arm spans or the masses of eggs from one farm, and most values sit near the middle, with fewer and fewer further out on either side. The smooth outline of that pile is the normal curve, often called the bell curve. Counts that pile up at 0, 1 and 2, and quantities with a long tail of large values, do not make it.

alt: A smooth, symmetric bell-shaped curve over a horizontal axis. A dashed line runs from the peak down to the axis, labelled mean = median = mode. The two tails, each labelled, run closer and closer to the axis without meeting it.
caption: Symmetric about the mean, highest at the mean, and tails that come closer and closer to the axis without touching it.

stem: Which of these would pile up in a bell: 200 adults' arm spans, the numbers of brothers and sisters in 200 families, the salaries in a large company?

steps.decision: Measured on a continuous scale, and gathered evenly around the average.
Small whole numbers that pile up at 0, 1 and 2, with a tail to the right.
Most near the lower end, with a long tail of a few very large values: skewed, not symmetric.

prompt: Which of these is most likely to follow a normal distribution?
options: The masses of eggs laid by one flock of hens
The number of pets in each household on a street
The times people wait for a train that comes exactly every 15 minutes
answer: The masses of eggs laid by one flock of hens
explain: As in step 1 of See it, a mass is measured on a continuous scale and gathers evenly around the average, so it makes a bell.

twin.prompt: Which of these would you expect to make a bell-shaped distribution?
options: The lengths of rainbow trout in one lake
The number of texts each pupil sends in a day
The prices of the cars for sale on a website
twin.answer: The lengths of rainbow trout in one lake
twin.explain: Length is continuous and gathers evenly around the average length.

optionNotes.option: The number of texts each pupil sends in a day
optionNotes.why: A count with a long tail of heavy users: skewed, not a bell.

optionNotes.option: The prices of the cars for sale on a website
optionNotes.why: A few very expensive cars make a long upper tail, as salaries do.

optionNotes.option: The number of pets in each household on a street
optionNotes.why: Small whole numbers piling up at 0, 1 and 2: not symmetric, like the brothers and sisters.

optionNotes.option: The times people wait for a train that comes exactly every 15 minutes
optionNotes.why: Every wait from 0 to 15 minutes is as likely as any other, so the shape is flat, not a bell.

md: The normal curve is symmetric about its mean and highest there. Its mean, median and mode are one number, with half the values on each side, and the whole area under the curve stands for all of the data, a fraction of 1.

title: Why the three averages agree
md: The mode is where the curve is highest, which is the centre. The median cuts the area in half, and by symmetry the two halves meet at the centre too. So the mean, the median and the mode are the same number.

alt: Two curves side by side. On the left, heights: a symmetric bell with one dashed line at its peak, labelled peak and mean. On the right, incomes: a curve that rises steeply, peaks early and has a long tail to the right; one dashed line marks the peak and another, further right, the mean.
caption: In the bell the peak and the mean are the same place. In a skewed shape like incomes, the long tail pulls the mean away.

stem: The lengths of a batch of shoes are normally distributed with mean 26.5 cm. Find the median and the mode, and the share longer than 26.5 cm.

steps.decision: The median halves the area, and the halves meet at the mean.
The curve is highest at the mean.
Symmetry puts the same share on each side.

prompt: The lengths of a batch of bolts are normally distributed with mean 48.6 mm. What is the median length, in millimetres?
explain: As in step 1 of See it, the median halves the area, and on a symmetric curve the halves meet at the mean: 48.6 mm.

twin.prompt: Pupils' reaction times are normally distributed with mean 0.31 seconds. What percentage of pupils take longer than 0.31 seconds?
twin.explain: Half the area lies on each side of the mean: 50%.

text: Why so many things are normal

md: A height or a mass is the sum of many small influences, each pushing a little up or a little down. A Plinko board does the same with balls: every peg pushes a ball left or right, and the bin it lands in adds up its pushes. Few paths reach the far bins and many reach the middle, so the bins fill into a bell.

stem: On a board with 10 rows of pegs, why does a middle bin fill far more than an end bin?

steps.working: An end bin needs every push the same way
steps.decision: Only one path of 10 pushes reaches it.

steps.working: A middle bin takes 5 pushes each way, in any order
steps.decision: Hundreds of different paths lead there.
So the middle fills most and the ends least: a bell.

title: PhET: Plinko Probability
attribution: Simulation by PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder, licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 (https://phet.colorado.edu)
task: Open the Lab screen and set the binary probability to 0.5. Start with 2 rows and drop a few hundred balls. Then add rows one at a time, up to the most the board allows, and drop a few thousand. Describe how the outline of the full bins changes.

prompt: On a Plinko board, what happens to the outline of the full bins as more rows of pegs are added?
options: It comes closer to a smooth, symmetric bell
It flattens, with every bin equally full
It leans over towards one side
answer: It comes closer to a smooth, symmetric bell
explain: As in step 3 of See it, each row adds one more small push, and the middle bins are reached by far more paths than the ends.

twin.prompt: A ball's final bin adds up 12 small pushes, each left or right with equal chance. Which bins fill most?
options: The bins at the two ends
twin.explain: Six pushes each way can come in many orders; all twelve one way only in one.

optionNotes.option: The bins at the two ends
optionNotes.why: An end bin needs all twelve pushes the same way: one path only.
The bins are reached by very different numbers of paths, so they cannot fill equally.

optionNotes.option: It flattens, with every bin equally full
optionNotes.why: The end bins have only one path each, so they can never fill like the middle.

optionNotes.option: It leans over towards one side
optionNotes.why: With pushes equally likely left and right, neither side is favoured.

text: Within one, two or three standard deviations

md: The standard deviation sets the width of the bell. Every normal curve keeps the same shares: about **68%** of the values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about **95%** within two, and about **99.7%** within three. A value more than three standard deviations from the mean is very unusual, though not impossible.

title: A check on every normal answer
md: The shares check later work too: the probability above a value two standard deviations over the mean should be near 2.5%, and the probability above the mean itself exactly a half.

alt: A normal curve with vertical lines at the mean μ and at one and two standard deviations either side. The bands hold 34.1% between the mean and one standard deviation on each side, 13.6% between one and two, and 2.3% in each tail beyond two. Brackets above mark about 68% within one standard deviation and about 95% within two.
caption: The shares in every normal curve: about 68% within one standard deviation, about 95% within two.

stem: The volumes of juice in cartons are normally distributed with mean 252 ml and standard deviation 1.5 ml. Find the ranges holding about 68% and about 99.7% of the cartons.

steps.decision: One standard deviation either side of the mean.
Three standard deviations either side: almost every carton.

steps.working: Each range is centred on the mean
steps.decision: Go the same number of standard deviations down as up.

prompt: Commuting times are normally distributed with mean 38 minutes and standard deviation 6 minutes. About 95% of the times lie between 26 minutes and what time?
explain: As in steps 1 and 2 of See it, but two standard deviations for 95%: $2 \times 6 = 12$, and $38 + 12 = 50$ minutes. The range is centred on the mean.

twin.prompt: The heights of a crop of sunflowers are normally distributed with mean 1.84 m and standard deviation 0.12 m. About 95% of them lie between what height and 2.08 m?
twin.explain: Two standard deviations either side: $1.84 - 2 \times 0.12 = 1.60$ m.

md: Because the curve is symmetric, every share splits evenly about the mean. The 32% outside one standard deviation lies in two equal tails, about 16% each; the 5% outside two gives about 2.5% in each tail. A band from the mean out to one side holds half of its two-sided share. Sketch the curve and shade the region first: the picture shows at once whether the share is small or large.

stem: For the juice cartons, find the share above 253.5 ml and the share above 255 ml.

steps.working: 253.5 ml is one standard deviation above the mean
steps.decision: Count the steps from the mean first.
The 32% outside splits into two tails.

steps.working: 255 ml is two above: $(100 - 95) \div 2 = 2.5$, so about 2.5%
steps.decision: Halve what lies outside two standard deviations.

prompt: Marks in a test are normally distributed with mean 62 and standard deviation 8. About what percentage of the marks lie between 62 and 70?
explain: As in step 2 of See it, use symmetry: 70 is one standard deviation above the mean, and the band from the mean to one side holds half of 68%, about 34%.

twin.prompt: For the same test, about what percentage of the marks lie between 62 and 78?
twin.explain: 78 is two standard deviations above; half of 95% is 47.5%.

md:
Recognise a bell: a measured quantity gathered evenly around its average.
Use mean = median = mode, half on each side, and a total area of 1.
Find the ranges holding about 68%, 95% and 99.7%.
Halve what lies outside for one tail: about 16% beyond one, 2.5% beyond two.

No paper has yet set the shape as a question of its own: it comes inside the normal question, with the mean and standard deviation given. The Summer 2019 report found that a sketch with the mean and the value marked under the axis made full marks far more likely, and saw some try the standard deviation formula, which is never needed there.
